"The Last Temptation of Christ"
How'm I supposed to start this out. I guess I'll begin with Scorses
item.description:
"The Last Temptation of Christ"
How'm I supposed to start this out. I guess I'll begin with Scorsese.
Martin Scorsese makes films I learn a lot from and appreciate his passion for, but don't particularly enjoy personally. Goodfellas is essential viewing. Casino is very decent. Shutter Island was good. Taxi Driver turned out okay. Mean Streets is just a proto-Goodfellas. And Wolf of Wall Street is just skippable, you don't need that in your life.
Come to find out he directed The Last Temptation of Christ, a nearly 3 hour film adaptation of a fictional work by a Greek Orthodox author. The book nearly got the author excommunicated; I don't know how one "fails" to get excommed, but that's what happened. When Scorsese adapted it to film, there was similar uproar amongst Christians of all traditions.
I'll address that next. The controversy. A lot of Christians protested the movie without having seen it. Lots of theaters refused to show it. When it came to television, stations received complaints. While I ultimately disagree with most of the protestors' criticisms, I do see where they're coming from. It deserved its R rating.
So believers rejected it. Apparently, The Passion of the Christ is inversely valid; the gore in that is acceptable, whereas in Temptation, the men kissing, full nudity, adult content, and seemingly blasphemous statements made by Jesus is not acceptable.
To be charitable, I'll consider the perceived blasphemy as the most egregious offense. Whenever Willem Dafoe's Jesus refers to himself as bad, a sinner, unfaithful, etc., it is not an accurate statement according to the Bible. ...Which is why at the very beginning of the film, Scorsese disclaims Biblical accuracy in the story. It's not one of the Gospel accounts. It's not holy writ. It's fiction. It's unfair to treat his story as true to the Word of God when he comes out at the front of the film stating irrevocably that it is not.
"Temptation" explores the human part of Jesus's dual nature: fully God and fully man. This is something all Christians believe. Scorsese is Catholic. I can't fathom why he would want to blaspheme his Savior whom he believes he consumes at every Mass. I don't believe Scorsese was bing ironic or whatever when making this film. I think he was taking the dual nature claim seriously, and venturing into the human side in a way that compels viewers to take it seriously too.
As for me and my wife, we're pretty exhausted with Jesus stories that come out stale before the DVDs are even packaged. Even "The Chosen" does this, in our opinion. At least "Passion" was rated R for its DOOM levels of bloody violence. That sets that apart.
"Temptation" suggests Jesus doesn't know who he is at the start. I intentionally leave "he" lowercase because I'm not talking about the Jesus of the Bible but the one in this movie. He has doubts about his purpose. He is enraptured with his destiny, stretched across and nailed to a piece of wood.
Something I noticed about this Jesus is he responded to different people differently. To Judas, played by Harvey Keitel, it's as though they're reaching in to find their inner street gangster. To Mary Magdalene, he is a sobbing mess. To his initial followers, he preaches awkwardly. To the demon-possessed lepers, he is a superhero, casting out spiritual forces left and right.
These different responses are so important because of the way each character interacts with this Jesus. More is revealed about the human talking to the son of man, than about Jesus himself. He is getting his audience to admit more about themselves. When Mary Magdalene says "You're just like all the others [men], you just don't admit it," it says a lot about her view of men, and very little about the Jesus she's talking to. The crowd that follows him around flees him in a frenzy. He tries to assuage them: "No no, I didn't say 'death!' I said 'love!'" Too late.

item.title: In fact, in revealing so much about the human characters, we viewers see just how un-divine, how non
item.description:
In fact, in revealing so much about the human characters, we viewers see just how un-divine, how non-deity, the humans are. We see how unlikely they are to carry their cross and follow Jesus. That's something Jesus told everyone to do. (Matthew 16:24, Luke 9:23, Mark 8:34) Nathaniel keeps worrying about his sheep. Judas wants to start the revolution against the Roman occupiers. But Jesus continually preaches about the all-importance of love. God is love, don't forget.
I have much more to say about this. We will watch this film again in a year or two. I'm grateful for a Jesus flick that doesn't merely give us a sanitized savior. Instead, The Last Temptation of Christ dares to go beyond our expectations, willing to seek something truly unique and artistic, while trying not to blaspheme the Creator.

item.title:
"We use what we protest"
It’s easy to find negative press surrounding AI data centers. There are pl
item.description:
"We use what we protest"
It’s easy to find negative press surrounding AI data centers. There are plenty of valid reasons for doing so: environmental effects, noise concerns, deceptive job offerings, etc. Then why are Google, Meta, and others even building these things in the first place? These buildings aren't simply constructed to sit around and occupy space.
The truth is there has to be something that entices massive corporations to spend hundreds of millions of dollars. They seek a return on their investment. Do we know what that return is?
I want to caution data center protestors on what exactly it is they're protesting. Any and all positives that data centers provide need to be outweighed by the negatives. One such "positive" is the increasingly ubiquitous use of AI in everyone's daily lives. If you run a Google search, you're using AI, you're creating demand for one of these data centers getting built. If you prompt ChatGPT to sift through reams of in-house procedures, you create demand for one of these data centers.
Perhaps we just don't know of the positives because we don't see them. When I worked at a copper mine, each truckload of shiny metal was a reminder of what we did, why we did it, how our work improved the lives of many, many others. That's not quite as obvious with an AI tool that generates a legal document in 30 minutes that normally takes several weeks and a few highly-trained individuals. (that's firsthand observation from an attorney, I didn't make that up) Or creating an app to help people crochet. (that's something my wife is working on now)
Examine how much we use AI at home and at work. We are driving the demand for the thing that we protest. You can try starving the demand, finding alternatives. But replacing Red 40 in our diet is much easier said and done than refusing to use ChatGPT.
We can't fairly judge the pros vs the cons of AI data centers without recognizing the pros. All the ways we use AI in our daily lives are "pros" whether we like them or not.

item.title:
“Citizen Vigilante”
When I heard the premise to this Uwe Boll (UB) movie, my mind immediately went
item.description:
“Citizen Vigilante”
When I heard the premise to this Uwe Boll (UB) movie, my mind immediately went to Death Wish. Man with no ties to hold him down goes around murdering bad guys, often of the minority variety. But this time, of course, there’s no Charles Bronson, automatically putting this at a disadvantage. Being a UB flick puts it at a further disadvantage.
I was not aware of the intense inner-city violence of the 1970s and 80s until I learned of the controversy surrounding the original Death Wish franchise. Michael Winner directed the second one, and the reason it took 8 years to go from 1 to 2 was this controversy. How dare it be so popular. There was an uproar. Bronson didn’t seem to mind it too much; he got paid, and he may have even agreed with Winner on the franchise’s principles.
It’s challenging to grow further-versed in cinema. We notice intentionality no matter how much garbage surrounds or results from it. Citizen Vigilante oscillates from pretty good to downright awful. Paul Kersey was a highly successful architect; Bruce Willis’s Kersey was a competent ER doc. Sanders (played by Armie Hammer) owns apartment buildings. And the bar underneath it. As well as the brothel somewhere in between.
The pacing is all over the place. From what little I’ve seen of UB, this is standard for him. Inconsistency abounds. One scene between Sanders and his direct report is the best so far, but not until after the incredibly long sex scene interrupted by Sanders’ manic attention to detail: there’s mold on the ceiling, of HIS building. He will monologue to petty thieves on the bus, before threatening one’s life. I can’t tell if this is a valid personality quirk of our main character, or UB stating his message way too obviously for us.
Is Sanders supposed to be autistic? ADD? OCD? CIA? I can’t tell. What darns me about this is that for all the blinding clarity, the actual messages seem impossible to decipher. Is Sanders a good guy with unfortunate psychopathic tendencies? Is Sanders a bad guy who’s just a racist who spent too much time radicalizing himself on right wing propaganda?
Ohp. He played “chicken” in the oncoming lane of a rural road. The innocent driver in the other vehicle veered off, tumbling twice. I said “It’s gonna blow up” right before it actually did, not expecting it. Even THAT, I thought UB would be above. There is no avoiding the tropes, sorry to dash your hopes.
The absolute worst shootout I’ve ever witnessed takes place in the man’s bunkered-up compound. Equally cringe is the three minute leadup to the event. I’m okay with actors who don’t have any SWAT training still gearing up in their plastic props and doing their best to appear authentic. These poor saps don’t look like they even tried. “Special” tactics, indeed.
I can only suspend so much belief.
The movie ends with a short monologue from the protagonist who is still at-large. UB posted an AI-generated image of the sequel, slated for next year (2027). There’s no way to conclude this is satire, as the final epigraph dedicates the movie to all the victims of crime committed by migrants. ...Oh, it doesn’t say that, it reads “dedicated to the thousands of rape and murder victims in Europe who were betrayed by our legal system.” To its narrow credit, the film is not racist, nor does it pin the ultimate blame on the migrants portrayed here. UB points to the legal system that didn’t do its job.
Also to its narrow credit, Citizen Vigilante is an unapologetically rightwing extremist film. It feels like leftwing extremist movies are free to abound, so pushing the boundary the other way deserves the barest modicum of praise, in my opinion.
It doesn’t follow that the movie is any good. 3/10

item.title:
"Mea Culpa (or, Check the Packaging)"
Wanting to talk more about this romance novel subject, but th
item.description:
"Mea Culpa (or, Check the Packaging)"
Wanting to talk more about this romance novel subject, but this is the third time in a week, so I better stop. Once I become "the guy who talks about that," I doubt I'd ever shake the accusation off.
So a final parting shot of advice. Now more than ever, it's important to be on guard against garbage for the eyes and the ears. We don't let our kids eat literal garbage with their mouths. We should not let them consume garbage with their eyes either. Feed them good media. "Furnish their minds with beauty," as Peter Hitchens said.
It's a good thing garbage tends to stink. We avoid the smell. When it's prettied up, people fall for it instead. In the UK, kids cereals can't have too attractive a logo. Should be eating their fruits and vegetables instead. There's concern here in the US of marijuana treats looking too much like harmless fruit snacks. Regardless of their effect on adults, when kids take them, they lead to hospitalization. The packaging is really similar without close examination.
Man, I gotta stop... I can just FEEL this connection I want to make. There's two wires that'll light up the path to the point I'm driving at. But there's a hundred others that, instead, will simply detonate me. And here I am prodding around with a screwdriver...
"From the fruit of his mouth a man is satisfied with good, and the work of a man's hand comes back to him." Proverbs 12:14 ESV

item.description:
"Romance Novels"
Perhaps my experience with romance in fiction is too limited for me to be considered anything more than woefully amateur. There are intimate scenes in Clancy, notoriously mocked by more serious readers, and they are graphic enough for my taste. It doesn't usually require me to skip the chapter, they're that short. The single Stephen King novel I read, there was initial intimacy and innuendo, and at least it moved the plot along.
Well, Hoopla recommended a novel from Elle Kennedy and I had the free borrow. I am also a grown man, darn it. I gave it a listen. Partway through, deleted, then redownloaded and continued. And another time. This content is not romantic, it is pornographic. The only difference between this and a spicy fanfiction is an editor.
I wasn't going to mention the author. Doing so makes it look like I'm singling her out. No. No, I'm not. There's many, many authors exactly the same as her. But her name popped up on my Audible too, with the notice that the book was going to be turned into a season on Amazon Prime.
As a matter of practical necessity, this visual adaptation will NOT be faithful to the book. A faithful adaptation would belong on OTHER streaming services. The ones you don't use work computers to look up.
Now, the book getting turned into an Amazon show is actually available to read, in full, online, for free. A simple Google search managed to bring up the thing, no viruses attached (to my knowledge). Even comes with a search function. I took the liberty of searching up various red flag terms so no one else reading this has to. Should you object to my listing of certain words, remember what I said earlier in this paragraph: it's all out there on the Web, no charge, no ID verification, nothing stopping anyone with temptation from indulging anyways. Instead, I'm going to assume you're an adult with discernment.
(Term - number of citations) Bulge - 2 out of 3 are erotic references Boobs - 2 Penis - 6 Orgasm - 14 Clit - 10 F*** - over 100
Look. There are many factors here beyond our control. Audible is going to continue hosting content like this. Romance novels will continue to showcase cover art that looks innocuous and PG, while its text is X rated. This doesn't at all exonerate visual pornography. All of this stuff is ridiculously easy to get to.
So parents: be hyper vigilant.

"Akira"
Back in college, some 15+ years ago, I watched Akira. My great anime sampling period. I wat
item.description:
"Akira"
Back in college, some 15+ years ago, I watched Akira. My great anime sampling period. I watched it, really enjoyed the animation, assumed it was pretty standard for high-end anime films, but was put off by how weird and confusing the story was. My wife and I watched it this week. She came to the same conclusion: excellent animation, glad she experienced it, content to never touch it again.
On the scale of 1 to Gross, this is about a 4.5. There's plenty of violence and mild gore up until the great transformation, where it becomes just freaking WEIRD. More unnerving, less discomfiting.
It's a classic. One of those you want to say you've seen without devoting the time and mental energy to see it. It's important historically. Fortunately, the animation is so good that that part alone makes the experience enjoyable. So yes. I do recommend Akira. Once.

item.description:
"Contentment"
I'm reading "The Rare Jewel of Christian Contentment" to the fam at dinner every night. We're only in chapter 2 and already my wife is seeing and applying the wisdom from it all over the place. This will be the... I think 4th time I'm going through it. Various versions exist; the audiobook narration is fairly archaic. There is an "original" version I gave someone and I regret that immensely. For our household, I got an updated English version. It is fairly literal in its translation, sticks to the rails of the original book, more like a copy-paste for every instance of "state" with "situation," that sort of thing. In any case, it's an excellent book, 10/10, would recommend to all and everyone. Every Christian would benefit from it.

item.title:
"Obligatory Unnecessaries"
It has not been "too long" that I've been putting off this topic. Rather
item.description:
"Obligatory Unnecessaries"
It has not been "too long" that I've been putting off this topic. Rather, it's that I waited till I had the right amount of time to get this all out in one, big go. (I'll still get interrupted here and there, oh well) How required is it of any piece of media to include a scene of excessive violence, gratuitous gore, non-stop swearing, extended sexuality, and detailed nudity? Is a movie no longer objectively good because the sex scene got taken out? Does a book need to include tons of curse words every page? What volume of blood is allowed per simulated killing? Which upskirts are okay? Which ones are not? At the risk of avoiding the question, I'm going to answer with a conditional statement: It depends on the audience. What's allowed for 5-year-olds should be very, very limited. What's allowed for a veteran is in many ways not at all limited, although PTSD may make certain content inappropriate for them too. What's allowed for a stable guy of mid-30s age should probably be just about unlimited. I suppose that does avoid the question. Sorry. That said, I think it's very important, and still pertinent. I would never show my kids Top Gun: Maverick. They drop the F-bomb at a clear and obvious point in the story. I would never play DOOM 2016 in front of them. They don't need to see that. And yet in my opinion both of those are 10/10's. So objectively good... for whom? There are some out there who are grossness-agnostic. Anything goes, doesn't matter to them. But what I find is that the more vocal proponents of hyper-gross material (Spine of Night, Heavy Metal) appear insistent on having the objectionable material in. Suggest they take it out? They will revert to the grossness-agnostic ("Why not? What's YOUR problem?"), but the truth is they argue it HAS to be in there. Because "It's just not the same without that part." Why not? Why is it suddenly different? Lesser? Chesterton's fence analogy comes to mind. The grossness-advocate may want to claim it applies to them, but the truth is it applies to the more moderate, more chaste, more prudent (prudish?) party. Before we include the ojbectionable content, we must recognize that it will break some fences. So before we remove those fences, we must understand the reason that fence was originally installed. Besides audience, we come back to objectivity. How much is too much? Well, that depends on what the "much" is and how it applies to the story and themes. Is it a war movie and meant to be super accurate? Expect language and violence. Is it set in feudal Japan? Prepare for some really weird kinks. So authenticity to the time period is acceptable. If there's absolutely no relation to the setting, then that should be an obvious omission. But say there's something objectionable yet applicable. I would say it's time to go back to the question of audience. Somehow, The Passion of the Christ invariably receives a free pass to all this discussion. N.D. Wilson says that when you reach the point in a movie or book where you actively think "God doesn't like this, He is displeased by this," that is when and where you should turn it off and put it away. Regardless of worldview, this is good advice. Don't engage in "vice tourism," as he puts it. What is the purpose of the objectionable content? All too often, it is not used as a supplement to the story or characters; rather, it is used to shock the audience. Artists love to do this. Same reason we ride roller coasters or watch anything horror-related. I have friends who review video games. They go through a lot of objectionable material in these titles. The purpose is to inform others before they make their own decision. Perhaps it's not strictly necessary that these reviewers exist, but it certainly benefits others.

item.title: My wife knew an attorney who had a case where he and a woman had to watch a movie frame by frame to
item.description: My wife knew an attorney who had a case where he and a woman had to watch a movie frame by frame to collect evidence of really, REALLY bad crimes. He was actively seeking it out. But why? To get a bad guy off the street. Any investiagtor has to deal with objectionable material all the time, for one of the most noble purposes out there. Where does this leave me? I think I want to start a series where I take out all the really awful stuff, the material I don't think is necessary, the grossness I believe is meant to shock and that's it, then see how well the film or book or game holds up. I would hope that consumers would pursue better media choices, and reject gratuitous grossness when it's encountered. In the meantime, as average consumers, I'd ask us to know our audience. Especially ourselves. Have a good idea of what constitutes "too far" for us individually. If we don't know ourselves, how can we expect someone else to know and abide by those sensibilities? If you're a creator, ask yourself: Why add this or that scene to your short film? Why include a verbal picture that lands outside of the societal "fence" built around it? It's commonly for a good reason why it's there in the first place.

item.title: "Megalopolis" Megalopolis is better than The Godfather at 1.5x speed, which is better than The Godfa
item.description: "Megalopolis" Megalopolis is better than The Godfather at 1.5x speed, which is better than The Godfather at normal speed, which is better than Apocalypse Now. I have only those three films of Coppola's to work with, but I'm content to say that much at least. I tried watching Godfather and couldn't get past 10 minutes. Decided to actually get through it, and when accelerated, it's actually pretty good. Apocalypse Now is due a rewatch if I'm gonna judge it fairly, but I was severely unimpressed when I checked it out after Full Metal Jacket. The Godfather represents one of those pieces of media that basically everyone you know says they've watched several times, probably had, and each time re-cemented their conclusion that it's one of the peaks of cinema. I'm sorry but it sounds like a lot of people ought to climb some more movie mountains. Get out of this little mafia hamlet of theirs and explore the surrounding cinematic countryside. Mount Godfather is not the only hill in the range. I make it a point to learn what popular standard has been set, then deliberately deviate away from it. If it doesn't work, I admit that the hype is right, and I course-correct. But too often, I find myself justified in veering away. So my wife pitched Megalopolis, telling me it was poorly-received by most of the public, and unavailable from pretty much every legal means (something we later learned was Coppola's doing as much as the film's unpopularity contributed to). Once again, we feel vindidacted for branching off. The film is visually stunning, each scene like a comic book panel from a fever dream Coppola had, which got recorded, retold, and recreated perfectly. It is intentionally weird, whereas other "true art" passion projects simply end up weirdly intentional. The pacing doesn't let up; over 2 hours and it still held our attention. Performances from all the cast of characters are stellar. Learning this was funded from Coppola's own wealth, this could have devolved into the kind of B-rate flick that Uwe Boll is known for (I vaguely remember a Medieval fantasy title - oh yeah, In The Name of The King - where the only one appearing to have a good time is Jason Statham, a credit to his unflappability). No, this is more like Drive: a high-caliber cast on a low-... budget set? Is that low-budget? It kinda looks like it. What's the opposite of "blockbuster?" Indie? Anyhow, Megalopolis is closer to Drive than to the other kind. Adam Driver and Shia LaBeouf in particular are directed impeccably, and they give their all for their roles. No one performed half-heartedly, like they didn't belong. We had read that this film felt more like a play than a movie. I actually disagree, though I get where they're coming from. There are cues and clues here and there which suggest a playwright, but it didn't hit me as blatantly as something like Fences. The story is very difficult to follow. It'll require a second and third watching for me to really understand it. It appears to wrap up very neatly at the end. As in Everything Everywhere All At Once, I very much appreciate the dedication to answering the central questions that the film asks. No "director ex machina" here, stuff happens, good guys win, doesn't elaborate, roll credits. No, Megalopolis concludes completely and definitively. I am grateful for that. The conclusions, however, I do find bothersome. Coppola doesn't appear to be an atheist. He grew up Catholic and has fallen away; his nuns are to blame. Possibly, he believes in a vague idea of spirituality. Without spoiling the very ending, it is a clear call to embrace a secular humanist future. (I'm sure the atheists will have to correct me on that; can't seem to ever get anything right according to them) And I don't mind appealing to clarity here because the very last shot is completely unambiguous in purpose. It is atheist and specifically secular humanist because it has no mention of God, no verbal recognition of Abrahamic religions ("Saturnalia" is used in a scene). Humanity is flying on its own fuel here.
